Symphony. An extended orchestral work, typically in three or four movements, that showcases the full resources of an ensemble through elaborate formal structures and thematic development. The symphony emerged as a distinct genre in the mid-eighteenth century from lighter Italian opera overtures, gradually expanding from a brief three-movement form into a substantial, independent concert work. It became the flagship form of Classical music and remains a central genre in orchestral repertoire.

The symphony evolved from the Italian sinfonia, an overture to operas, which gradually expanded into its own form. The typical four-movement structure consists of an Allegro, fast and in sonata form; an Andante, slow; a Minuet and Trio, or Scherzo in later symphonies; and a final Presto or Allegro in fast rondo or sonata form. The first movement typically employs sonata form, presenting two contrasting themes, developing them through harmonic and rhythmic variation, and recapitulating them in a final resolution.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote forty-one numbered symphonies, establishing the Classical symphonic ideal: elegant proportion, memorable themes, and virtuosic orchestration while maintaining formal clarity. Ludwig van Beethoven transformed the symphony into a vehicle for profound philosophical and emotional statement, expanding it beyond Classical conventions; his nine symphonies are regarded as the pinnacle of the form.

Romantic-era composers including Hector Berlioz, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, and Anton Bruckner expanded the symphony in scope, duration, and orchestral resources, exploring program music and unprecedented harmonic complexity. The symphony declined somewhat in the early twentieth century as other forms gained prominence, but composers including Dmitri Shostakovich, Aaron Copland, and Leonard Bernstein revitalized the form with new expressive possibilities.
